content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors argue that many applications of ASR require an orthographic transcription with case and punctuation. Moreover, a generic ASR system should work in various acoustic conditions. A truly end-to-end ASR system should therefore have good performance for different audio and text distributions with their variations (punctuation, normalization, speaker variations etc) without changing their pre- or post-processing strategy.

This paper proposes an end-to-end speech challenge benchmark to test ASR against these variations. The benchmark is made of several already publicly available datasets representing the different conditions. Five state-of-the-art ASR systems are evaluated with this benchmark. The macro average of word error rate (WER) and orthographic WER (including punctuation and casing) are computed and differences between systems are analysed and discussed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: Evaluating ASR systems on various datasets to claim SOTA (rather than librispeech only for example) is a good idea and should be encouraged as a good practice in the field. A common benchmark is quite a good idea and provide researchers with a way to compare systems, as it is the case in NLP for example.

Weaknesses: The novelty is quite limited: the proposed benchmark is made of existing datasets only and no new method, model, ... is proposed. Moreover, systems trained to output punctuation will always do so even for dataset that did not include them in the transcript. However, one needs a common convention for evaluation (e.g. punctuation removal when the ground-truth doesn't have it), and it is not clear in the paper for example whether the transcribed text is normalized to evaluate on Librispeech (I guess it is..)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is pretty clear, well written and easy to follow. 
There are maybe many unnecessary repetitions of the same statement about diversity of speech and texts and need for general ASR. 
The way the systems are evaluated when the ground-truth is normalized is not clear (cf. previous section).

This proposal could establish a common ground for evaluation and enforce good evaluation practice in the ASR community, but the novelty is quite limited: all the presented datasets already exist and the metrics are standard. 

Minor issues:
  Table 7: first column should be "Train"
content.summary_of_the_review:
The idea presented in this paper is good: ASR systems presented in papers are often evaluated on either private datasets or only in some conditions. If we aim at achieving good general accuracy for ASR systems, it is crucial to have a complete enough benchmark, which is proposed in this paper.

However, the relevance of evaluating ASR models predicting orthographic form on datasets for which the ground-truth does not include case and punctuation could be discussed, and the evaluation procedure could be clearer in that regard. 

It would also be interesting to see different systems (like cascaded ASR, or systems that include punctuation restoration) in the benchmark.

The paper do not include any new dataset, metric or model, making its novelty limited.

For these reasons, I think that the paper is below the acceptance threshold for ICLR, but would make an excellent contribution at ICASSP, Interspeech or other more ASR-focused conferences.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper5042 by Reviewer PhhZ

content.title: Response to Reviewer PhhZ
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for their valuable comments and appreciate their acknowledgement for the relevance of such a benchmark for the speech community. 

The ESC benchmark contains datasets with three different transcription formats: normalised, punctuated, punctuated and cased (orthographic). Submitted systems are trained and evaluated on each of the individual datasets in turn. When a system is trained on a normalised dataset (e.g. LibriSpeech), it is trained to predict normalised transcriptions. When it is subsequently trained on an orthographic dataset (e.g. SPGISpeech), it is trained to predict orthographic transcriptions. In both cases, the objective is to train the system to predict transcriptions that match the formatting requirements of the target text. Under the dataset-agnostic approach, systems have no a-priori knowledge of whether the transcriptions should be normalised or orthographic. Systems are instead required to learn this from the training data in an entirely data-driven way.

For all transcription formats (normalised or orthographic), systems are evaluated using the orthographic WER metric, as defined in the paper. For normalised transcriptions, there is no casing or punctuation in the ground truths. As such, trained systems should predict transcriptions accordingly. By nature of the orthographic WER, erroneous casing or punctuation in the predictions is penalised:

| Ground truth (normalised): | “the cat sat on the mat”|
|----------------------------|---------------------------|
| **Prediction:**                | **“The cat sat on the mat”**|


=> substitution error (“the” -> “The”)

For orthographic transcriptions, trained systems should predict the correct casing and punctuation in the transcriptions. The same orthographic WER is applicable for orthographic transcriptions, penalising incorrect casing or punctuation in the same way as for normalised:

| Ground truth (ortho): | “The cat sat on the mat .”|
|----------------------------|---------------------------|
| **Prediction:**                | **“The cat sat on the mat ”**|

=> deletion error (“.” -> “ ”)

By action of the orthographic WER, we are able to assess the system for different transcription requirements under the same metric.

We recognise that the paper is very focussed on the speech domain, and as such is likely more suited to a speech conference. Consequently, we are withdrawing the paper from ICLR, and will instead look towards a more speech-related venue. We again thank the reviewer for their encouraging comments and clarifying questions.

- Study the accent of the speakers, or the speaker demographics in general and propose a new test set based on that.
- Study on the quality of the transcripts to propose a new set, like Librispeech with test-clean and test-other

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper5042 by Reviewer KonF

content.title: Response to Reviewer KonF
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their comments. We acknowledge that evaluating ASR systems on multiple datasets is not a new concept. However, this is not done by all works and not in a unified manner. Works typically use different evaluation datasets and different pre-/post-processing. This prevents the comparison of systems performance across works. This paper seeks to address this problem by introducing a new ASR benchmark that rigorously defines the constraints on system evaluation. In this regard, the ESC benchmark aims to unite ASR researchers by assembling 10 existing datasets to form a new benchmark for ASR evaluation, in a comparable way to GLUE [1] and SuperGLUE [2] in NLP.

We would politely like to draw the reviewer’s attention to three aspects of the paper we believe to be novel:

1. Unifying 10 individual ASR datasets that cover 11 different domains to form a multi-domain benchmark that encapsulates different ASR conditions. This is in contrast to many existing works that evaluate systems on different datasets with different pre- and post-processing.

2. Inclusion of all aspects of orthography (punctuation and casing) in the transcription requirements, encouraging systems capable of predicting orthographic outputs. This is in contrast to most existing works that normalise transcriptions and predict un-cased and un-punctuated outputs.

3. A dataset-agnostic approach, requiring systems trained with no a-priori knowledge of the data distributions. This is in contrast to the dataset-specific typically employed by most existing works, with ASR systems that optimise for single dataset performance. Thus, ESC encourages more generalisable, multi-domain speech systems.

[1] Alex Wang, Amanpreet Singh, Julian Michael, Felix Hill, Omer Levy, and Samuel R. Bowman. GLUE: A Multi-Task Benchmark and Analysis Platform for Natural Language Understanding. In 7th International Conference on Learning Representations, ICLR 2019, New Orleans, LA, USA, May 6-9, 2019. OpenReview.net, 2019. URL https://openreview.net/forum?id=rJ4km2R5t7.

[2] Alex Wang, Yada Pruksachatkun, Nikita Nangia, Amanpreet Singh, Julian Michael, Felix Hill, Omer Levy, and Samuel Bowman. SuperGLUE: A Stickier Benchmark for General-Purpose Language Understanding Systems. In H. Wallach, H. Larochelle, A. Beygelzimer, F. d'Alche ́-Buc, E. Fox, and R. Garnett (eds.), Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, volume 32. Curran Associates, Inc., 2019. URL https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2019/file/4496bf24afe7fab6f046bf4923da8de6-Paper.pdf.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper authors introduce the end-to-end speech challenge (ESC) for evaluating automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems across a broad set of speech datasets. This paper summarizes details of the included speech datasets, evaluation methodology, benchmarking results of several end-to-end (E2E) ASR systems, and analysis.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: This proposed ESC provides a good benchmark platform for the speech community to evaluate and compare systems, which helps facilitate speech technology development. Overall this paper is clearly written, including details of datasets and benchmark results and analysis.

Weakness: I find this paper has limited technical innovation. While ESC has its values for the broad speech community, this paper mainly focuses on summarizing existing datasets and setting up baselines with existing E2E ASR systems, with limited contribution to new technology development.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper clearly presents authors's work, and it is reproducible with public datasets and baselines systems.
content.summary_of_the_review:
As said above, this proposed ESC has its potentials to serve as a standard benchmark for ASR, which benefits the speech community. However, I find it has limited technical innovation. 

There are also several questions which I'd suggest authors consider addressing:

1. In the first paragraph of Section 7, it's said "On Earnings-22 and AMI, CTC + n-gram performs worse than CTC." This is different from general observations that adding a language model helps CTC performance. Do authors have thoughts on why this is the case?
2. The ESC score is defined based on WER. For this case, a high ESC score means worse performance. This seems to be different from general notion that a high score represent better performance.
3. As explained in Section 5, an unweighted average of WERs is calculated as the ESC score. Those datasets with worse WER metrics (and related bigger WER changes) could potentially dominate. Are there further thoughts on how to balance the impacts of different datasets in the final score?
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper5042 by Reviewer h1XK

content.title: Response to Reviewer h1XK
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their insightful comments and appreciate their remarks on the potential of the benchmark for the speech community.

The main contribution of the paper is rigorously defining a new ASR benchmark, assembling 10 datasets from 11 different domains into one unified benchmark and pairing them with a motivated methodology for evaluation. We select existing datasets that are widely considered to be the most relevant and applicable datasets by the research community. We evaluate five SoTA baseline systems on the benchmark in order to assess how relevant ASR systems perform across these tasks. The benchmark aims to encourage better evaluation of ASR systems across different audio conditions and transcription requirements.
In this regard, the contribution is similar to GLUE [1] or SuperGLUE [2], benchmarks in the NLP domain that assemble the most relevant NLP tasks into one benchmark, without introducing new datasets, tasks or models, but rather using those that are well-established in the NLP literature. These benchmarks aim to encourage better evaluation of NLP systems across different tasks, uniting NLP researchers under one shared objective.

In response to the reviewer's questions:

1. The n-gram language models are trained on the word frequencies in the training set for each dataset. Earnings-22 and AMI are the two smallest datasets in the benchmark, with 105h and 78h of training data respectively (see Table 1). Both datasets also have cased and punctuated transcriptions. The relatively worse performance of CTC + n-gram is likely due to the difficulty in aggregating statistics of words with punctuation and casing from small text corpora: every version of a word with punctuation or casing is a new vocabulary item. Thus, word frequencies and, by extension, word probabilities are low for punctuated or cased words. This suggests that training LMs on a large amount of data is beneficial, and external data should be used when the dataset is small.

2. We sought to remain consistent with the ASR literature with our choice of metric. Since the WER is ‘de facto’ choice of metric for assessing ASR systems, we opted for a benchmark score that reflects the WER of the constituent datasets. In that respect, a lower ESC score is better, in the same way that a lower WER is better. We will consider alternative metrics, such as word accuracy, for revised editions.

3. The datasets with higher WERs are the more challenging ones (e.g. GigaSpeech). We wish to encourage multi-domain ASR systems that fare equally well on the harder datasets as the easier ones (e.g. LibriSpeech). Thus, the unweighted average provides an in-built mechanism for regularising scores: contributions are naturally greater for the harder datasets and lesser for the easier ones, encouraging systems to improve on the harder datasets for better ESC scores.

Given the heavy focus of the paper on the speech recognition domain, we have decided to withdraw the paper from ICLR. We will look to address the reviewer’s pertinent questions in any future submission of this work. We again thank the reviewer for their comments and questions.

[1] Alex Wang, Amanpreet Singh, Julian Michael, Felix Hill, Omer Levy, and Samuel R. Bowman. GLUE: A Multi-Task Benchmark and Analysis Platform for Natural Language Understanding. In 7th International Conference on Learning Representations, ICLR 2019, New Orleans, LA, USA, May 6-9, 2019. OpenReview.net, 2019. URL https://openreview.net/forum?id=rJ4km2R5t7.

[2] Alex Wang, Yada Pruksachatkun, Nikita Nangia, Amanpreet Singh, Julian Michael, Felix Hill, Omer Levy, and Samuel Bowman. SuperGLUE: A Stickier Benchmark for General-Purpose Language Understanding Systems. In H. Wallach, H. Larochelle, A. Beygelzimer, F. d'Alche ́-Buc, E. Fox, and R. Garnett (eds.), Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, volume 32. Curran Associates, Inc., 2019. URL https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2019/file/4496bf24afe7fab6f046bf4923da8de6-Paper.pdf.

This work addresses the problem that an end-to-end speech recognition model may not generalize well on multi-domain setup, and proposes a benchmark that combines multiple speech tasks. The paper also evaluates a few different end-to-end models on the proposed benchmark.
There are some related works that are missing, like:
Toward Domain-Invariant Speech Recognition via Large Scale Training. SLT 2018.
RNN-T models fail to generalize to out-of-domain audio: Causes and solutions. SLT 2019.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: multi-domain is an important issue for speech recognition, and having an open benchmark highlights its importance and can encourage the community to focus on improving end-to-end models for this direction.
Weakness: this is a pretty speech-domain-focused paper, and will be a good fit for a speech conference, but ICLR is not the best venue for this paper.
